A small language for Linux operations

Linux automation you can explain.

Small Linux automation scripts grow in a predictable way: validation, quoting, branching, file publication, service changes, and failure handling accumulate around a few familiar commands. yesh keeps that surrounding procedure visible, so you can review what it checks, changes, and leaves untouched before it runs.

    install -m 0640 -- config.next /etc/myapp.conf.next

PLAN validate → prepare → publish → restart → verify

The review standard

Before running a small operational script, an operator should be able to answer five simple questions:

  1. What does it check first?
  2. What exact arguments reach each process?
  3. Which files or services can change?
  4. What happens if a command fails halfway through?
  5. What remains unchanged?

About

Bash is excellent for interactive work, short glue, and composing Unix programs. yesh is for the awkward middle: a script too important to hide behind shell tricks, but too close to the Linux command line to justify a larger framework.

Python and Ansible still solve different problems. yesh keeps the real Linux command visible and makes the procedure around it easier to inspect.

Before it runs

Commands are executed directly, not rebuilt into a string for sh -c. The same parsed script can show the concrete work before anything starts:

yesh --plan examples/service-restart.yesh
PLAN ["grep" "-q" "^mode=production$" "config.next"]
PLAN ["install" "-m" "0640" "--" "config.next" "/etc/myapp.conf.next"]
PLAN publish "/etc/myapp.conf.next" to "/etc/myapp.conf"

Current work

Where yesh fits

  • Backup and publicationCoordinate rsync, storage checks, locking, publication, reruns, and recovery.
  • Service diagnosisAsk systemd or OpenRC for a bounded state, journal, process, or resource snapshot.
  • Networked operationsKeep SSH, SCP, rsync, DNS, routes, and remote paths visible as external tools.

What it is not

It is not a shell replacement, a fleet manager, an orchestrator, or a resident monitoring agent. It does not replace Ansible’s inventory, roles, desired state, or multi-host coordination. yesh is a clear operation for one node, or one understandable step inside a larger automation system.

“What does it check? What command does it run? What remains if it fails?”

Bash comparison

This is the same incremental backup procedure in both languages: check the snapshot root, refuse an existing destination, copy into a private directory with rsync, then publish the completed tree. The Bash version is a careful baseline, not a caricature.

examples/bash-rsync-incremental-baseline.sh

set -Eeuo pipefail
IFS=$'\n\t'

die() { printf 'error: %s\n' "$*" >&2; exit 1; }
trap cleanup EXIT

[[ -d $root ]] || die "snapshot root is missing"
[[ ! -e $current ]] || die "snapshot already exists"
[[ ! -e $temporary ]] || die "temporary path already exists"

exec 9>"$lock" || die "cannot open lock"
flock -n 9 || die "another backup holds the lock"
mkdir -- "$temporary"

rsync_args=(-a --fsync --delay-updates)
[[ -e $previous ]] && rsync_args+=(--link-dest="$previous")
rsync "${rsync_args[@]}" -- "$source" "$temporary/"
mv -- "$temporary" "$current"

examples/rsync-incremental.yesh

if exists "/backup":
    if exists "/backup/snapshot.1":
        echo "current snapshot already exists"
        exit 3
    else:
        if exists "/backup/.snapshot.1.tmp":
            echo "temporary snapshot already exists"
            exit 4
        else:
            with lock "/run/lock/app-backup.lock":
                if exists "/backup/snapshot.0":
                    rsync -a --fsync --delay-updates --link-dest "/backup/snapshot.0" -- "/srv/app/" "/backup/.snapshot.1.tmp"
                else:
                    rsync -a --fsync --delay-updates -- "/srv/app/" "/backup/.snapshot.1.tmp"
                publish "/backup/.snapshot.1.tmp" to "/backup/snapshot.1"

The difference is not that yesh replaces rsync. It makes the preconditions, lock, failure boundary, and publication step part of the readable procedure. Read the Bash baseline · Read the yesh scenario · See the documentation

Small systems and notes

Alpine is a useful reference case: a small image may have musl, BusyBox, and OpenRC rather than systemd, and a full Bash installation is not a safe assumption. A network operation may have only the SSH features it actually needs.

yesh is distributed as a small statically linked Go binary. That is a good fit for this kind of work: the operational image does not need a language runtime, a shell framework, or a package of hidden helpers. Put the binary beside the specific external tools the procedure requires, and its execution boundary stays easy to inspect.

For this environment yesh can be a separate static operational image. It does not restore a shell or become another init system. It coordinates one bounded operation with the external tools that are explicitly present.

Resource observation is deliberately finite. A scenario can identify the service and its supervisor, collect process and cgroup data, read a bounded part of the journal, and save a JSONL record for later comparison. A summary can show whether memory or process behaviour changed across those records.

This is useful for a diagnosis or a deployment check because the script leaves a small, inspectable account of what was observed. It is not a background collector: it does not poll forever, keep a central state store, or replace a monitoring system.
